utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. On this day, the 16th of April, 2007, I would like to greet everyone in the courtroom. We are unfortunately 10 minutes late, but this delay was not due to us. I would like to greet the Prosecution, ladies and gentlemen of the Defence, as well as the accused. Before handing the floor to Mr. Prlic, I would like to first give the floor to the registrar for our IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Several parties have submitted lists of documents to be entered through Witness Herbert Okun. The list submitted by the OTP shall be given the Exhibit number IC 522. The list submitted by 1D shall be given Exhibit number IC 523. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit number IC 524. The list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number IC 525, while the list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit number IC 526. That's everything, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Prlic, if you wish to say something, you may go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'm going to address a number of issues, most of them linked to procedural matters, as was the agenda of the meeting you had on the 27th -- 22nd of March. I'd like to say that my sole request from the first time I appeared here in court was to ask that the trial be a fair one, that fair proceedings and just proceedings be secured, and I must say that on that score I'm becoming more and more concerned, and that is what -- the reason for which I have decided to take the floor. I am of course speaking only in my own name. I have not consulted anybody, and that includes my Defence counsel. So everything that I say, be it good or be it bad, is of my own utterance. Now, part of the -- some of the accused have asked me to speak in their own name, too, but I refused to do so, and that is my first message when I address procedural matters and that is that the indictment and the whole proceedings would have to be -- will have to be individual for each person. That is why I ask the Trial Chamber not to treat us as a group. A few days ago on television I heard a representative of the Prosecution, Nikiforov, who said that the criminal enterprise or joint criminal enterprise was a legal concept which enables a number of persons to be held accountable and to be accused, or, rather, to place a whole group of people under one indictment, or, as is stated in submissions, the most senior surviving person in our case. So this in fact shows the basic reason. All the rest is technology, law of custom and so on and so forth. I read the transcript of the 22nd of March, and at first glance it would appear that the subjects that were discussed were very ordinary. However, as we are weighing up justice here, they are basic fundamental questions, and I'm going to say a few words about each of the individual subjects discussed. First of all, I'd like to say that I have to notice that my Defence asked for this hearing to be convened. However, afterwards, according to the agenda -- the agenda that we had, it was the Prosecution's proposals that were put forward on the agenda. So I'm going to address the subject, the so-called means by which to speed up the trial. Now, the first of these means are the adjudicated facts. I think that after one year of trial that it has become clear to everyone, including the members of the Trial Chamber, why the Defence teams did not accept proposals for adjudicated facts. First and foremost, the previous Trial Chambers took decisions about matters which in their cases and trials represented either the context for something or was something they needed to prove that the conflict was of an international character so as to be able to apply Article 2 of the Statute, and here these are the most important elements of the criminal enterprise. Now, in these cases, the Defence teams did not deal with these things. They were not interested whether the HVO, for example, was a civilian authority or whether it was the name of an army, a military group, what the goals of Croatia were and what the goals of Herceg-Bosna were. Now, if we look at everything that was included in the judgements, and I'm just referring to the conflicts, not the crime base, so -- I went through the judgements over the past few days, and I'm bearing in mind what we have heard over the past year, everything is questionable, and also the jurisdiction which we try to rely upon. I don't wish to comment the discussions and debates that were held two weeks ago about Vares as being an adjudicated fact or facts, because Judge Prandler explained his position. Of course one of the basic criteria for accepting in formal terms these facts is, is that it was not based on an agreement as to recognition of liability and admission of guilt, and all the discussions about time are relative, including discussions which are being waged in this particular trial as well, and they speak to the fact that in my opinion the burden of proof has been shifted to the Defence increasingly frequently. It is not sufficient to say that it is only up to the Prosecution, that the Prosecution has the burden of proof, but daily decisions have to be made which confirm that principle. Now, your decision to accept adjudicated facts of the 14th of September tells us that this stage in which the Prosecution presents proof and evidence is almost unnecessary. Everything becomes cumulative and can only help the Defence teams like the last witness before the Easter break did to refute those theses. The Defence could start the process straight away and save resources, if that is something that must be uppermost in our minds. But let me remind you of the first four acts which were adjudicated by you, and I'd like you to listen carefully. I'm going to quote from page 15 of the ruling of the 14th and 23rd of June, 2006, pursuant to a Prosecution submission about formally accepting facts that have already been adjudicated. The first is this: The HVO became the supreme defence and executive body of the HZ HB and the BH Croats. That meant that in that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina real power and authority was held by the HZ HB. Now the second, and I quote: There is no doubt that the Republic of Croatia and the HZ HB had the same ultimate goal, and that was to join up the Croatian provinces of Bosnia-Herzegovina to a uniform and united Croatian state. The third is the following: Despite the fact that they knew that the other parties had not signed but relying on the fact that they had international public support, the BH Croats endeavoured unilaterally to implement the Vance-Owen Plan. And fourth, the fourth point, is this: On the territory to which the indictment refers, there was a systematic and widespread attack on the Muslim population in the area. This campaign had a concrete task, to transform the previously ethnically mixed area in Mostar, in and around Mostar, into a Croatian area with an ethnically pure population of BH Croats. And to this I would like to add that the first and third of these facts were adjudicated by this Trial Chamber, although the Pre-Trial Chamber on the 14th of March rejected it. So six months after the presentation of this case, this Trial Chamber considers that these standpoints and positions are facts which the Prosecution in these proceedings need not prove. Well, what do they have to prove then if not that? What can one say after all this? It seems that the Prosecution has to finish presenting its evidence. That is in store for us within the completion strategy, because the burden of proof almost before the trial ever began was transferred, it would seem, to the Defence, because when we do have witnesses, Prosecution witnesses, to testify about those matters, as a rule not enough time is given to the Defence for their cross-examination. The first four mentioned adjudicated facts, in my opinion, are sufficient for a judgement to be reached and made without the Prosecution having to say a single word. Of course, on condition that the Defence counsel don't engage either. As we're dealing with questions which are linked to the joint criminal enterprise, and we are witness that part of the defence of the accused here do not deal to any great extent with those questions. At least they haven't done so thus far. And I am speaking exclusively theoretically and hypothetically. I hope nobody will take this amiss. So does that mean that a judgement can already be brought in, made? Now, the second question that I'd like to talk about is agreed facts. I was -- in a bona fide attempt to prone -- to have accepted most of the facts that present a crime base, although I must recognise that I am changing my opinion when I see some of the exhibits and evidence that is endeavoured to be presented, such as sniper action and similar things; that is, events that are not sufficiently known. But I cannot believe the Prosecution fully either when it comes to crime base matters. Now, what is the basic premise in all this? We cannot accept a formulation according to which the HVO forces and HVO authorities that this is equal and that they have allegedly done something, committed something. Every crime must have a perpetrator, and all the elements must have been proved, which is customary in any court of law and legal proceedings. En passant I have a question to ask in this regard perhaps to enrich the Tribunal as well. I wanted to ask for a closed session for me 10 days ago for example when the question was rape was discussed. We had a mother here whose daughter was raped. The public gallery was full. There were just three of us here because of the flu epidemic, and sponsored television programmes broadcast this, and at that time I was already convict because the young people sitting in the public gallery who might well have been my students became convinced listening to the debate, which was sometimes in open session and sometimes in closed session to add a dramatic element to the proceedings, that it is we or me or us who were the perpetrators. Now, when it comes to protected witnesses, once again I'd like to say this en passant because it's not something that really affects me, although I consider we have gone too far because the same people are testifying about perpetrators in Bosnia-Herzegovina and I seem to gain the impression that it is portrayed as the Wild West, and I already intervened on that score on one occasion because that is not what the situation is like. So we -- that should not be the message sent out from this Tribunal. We must have a clear-cut mission when speaking about things having been done in the region. So these people are testifying down there and here objectively where the perpetrators have not been brought to trial in proceedings which should be -- have an open character are protected witnesses and their testimonies heard in closed session. Now, how can we defend ourselves from that? My Defence counsel are not asking this question. What should we do theoretically to find the perpetrators, to bring them here into the courtroom, to state their names loud and clear? Nobody seems to know them. So what is the standard of proof in that regard for something to be accepted as having been a crime? The indictment is as it stands. We seem to be responsible for everything under, as the Prosecution calls it, the leader's indictment in view of the formulations of the HVO authorities and HVO forces. Everything comes under those concepts and terms, it would appear. And I apologise for this comparison, I don't want to say anything bad by making the comparison, but it seems to me that it would be as if the Secretary-General of the United Nations who at a certain stage concluded that this type of indictment should be used, that he should be responsible for everything that happens in the world, that the Secretary-General should be responsible for everything. Even with the agreed facts when this sentence is not challenged or term is not challenged which is something the Prosecution mentioned and I agree with that, especially in view of the previous context, one can gain a quite different impression. The third element are documentary facts and elements and exhibits, and I consider that generally accepted facts can be accepted such as the Official Gazettes, for example. However, we see that the material and documents of international organisations with various judgements made without the people that compiled them cannot be accepted per se, and this we saw with the events in Stupni Do, for example, and the documents pertaining to that event. So it's very important to have a witness that you can test and cross-examine and put contradictory statements to as well. Or your decision on accepting the testimony from Gornji Vakuf, though it doesn't personally really affect me. It's part of the crime base. But I only mention it for one reason. It is stated that the same facts are in question which the Defence had occasion to check with other witnesses through their cross-examination. Again the question remains, was there enough time for this, or the rather offhand acceptance of the vocabulary of the Prosecution who use the term "HVO ultimatums" in accepting certain decisions. And again, the presumption of innocence is being overlooked, or something that the Judges often underline, and that is that it is the -- up to the Prosecution to prove its case. And I quote from page 11 of your decision in response to the motion of the Prosecution for the admission of evidence again about Gornji Vakuf. I think pursuant to Rule 92 bis (A) and (B) of the Rules of Procedure, and I quote: "Anyway, the Trial Chamber wishes to specify that the Defence will be able to present new evidence and documents during the presentation of the case of the Prosecution." I think this is a mistake. I think it should be the case of the Defence because there are no such witnesses of the Prosecution. And also, this decision says that those transcripts are being admitted because the perpetrators are far removed from the accused, which implicitly means that the criminal enterprise remains the basic form of responsibility. Let us recall the adjudicated facts that I have already discussed. In principle, evidence should be admitted through witnesses. Let there be a better selection. Let all parties focus more. If we depart from that principle, nothing will be achieved, and we will all remain in a mist, in a fog. Of course, I have not been studying the Rules of Procedure closely since the trial has begun, though I did study it before. I simply read through the decisions of other Trial Chambers, and there are so many changes, amendments, bises, and ters, so that this has become a kind of al a carte approach through which almost anything can be proven and disproven, but it is again within the discretion of the Trial Chamber, which also carries the main responsibility. So my conclusion in connection with these three auxiliary means, we must not allow due to shortage of time to succumb to the pressure of admission of adjudicated facts and documentary evidence without enough attention being devoted to them. A few words about time. Nothing is too small or too big unless compared with something else. In a period since the adoption of the indictment and the final judgement, it will be some five years. Discussing this matter with people outside the court, ordinary people who are relatively well-informed, it -- finds it difficult for them that so much time is needed for a trial. Regardless of that, as is common knowledge, I have renounced my right to a speedy trial, an expedited trial, because that right has seriously jeopardised my right to a fair trial. I do not wish to speak about the indictment. We have the lawyers for that. We have tried to make it clearer through all our preliminary submissions. All of them were rejected, which I think has put this Trial Chamber confronted with a lot of difficulty. I wish to state very clearly I do not wish the possibility of the Prosecution to do its utmost to present its version of the indictment to be overcast by any kind of shadow. As they say themselves, they have been working on it for some 10 years. We are taking adjudicated facts from other cases. An enormous amount of funds has been -- have been invested into this case. I do not wish to debate that, but I do ask that the Prosecution be allowed to present its case to the end, that they be given the opportunity to work. I personally wish to praise them for their diligence but not for any unlimited ambition. For example, in the appeal about your decision regarding time, in paragraph 3 they point out, and I will read it in English. "[In English] In a very real way, the Prlic case is the Karadzic plus Plavsic plus Krajisnik plus Martic plus two other cases rolled into one single case." [Interpretation] End of quote. What can be said? When talking about procedure and the proceedings, I have several requests to make. The first is the one that I have already taken the floor, and I wish to use a notebook during the proceedings. As the word itself says, a notebook means a simple notebook in the twenty-first century, so that my people in the Defence can take it from me and bring it back at the end of the day. I mean a notebook computer. I don't understand why this was not allowed, especially as I cannot sit next to my Defence counsel. My other request was to have enough time for cross-examination for some 10 or so witnesses to challenge their thesis, because if the Trial Chamber finds that the Prosecution has not proven the indictment, then there will be no need for my defence, and this will only gain time. I wonder whether my rights have been absolutely, seriously in jeopardy. There is had no my case here. The Prosecution needs to profits case. That is, that -- if it were my case I would prepare it differently. However, here it is adjusted to the indictment. In principle, my lawyer is not able to it use more than 10 per cent of the questions that I feel need to be put to witnesses. I am talking about those talking about the context of the criminal enterprise including the witness prior to the Easter holidays who I believe was a very good witness who could have clearly shown whether there was a criminal enterprise or not, of course, if there had been time to have his reports and his diary admitted. And on that basis, any officer of the Chamber could have prepared an opinion for this Trial Chamber. Instead of us discussing for a whole year this criminal enterprise, we could have done it in a much shorter period of time. Also, when talking about time, I think that the time given to the Prosecution for cross-examination is an unfair decision. We are not any kind of group. We may not eventually use more than one-sixth of the time. I don't know that. But fixing the limits among the Defence counsels is no solution. I talked to the other accused about other cases, and there is no similar limitation of time for cross-examination in other cases. I fear that sometimes the clock is becoming the main instrument here, and bargaining with time among the Defence counsels of the accused here has become the basic, and I hope you don't mind if I say so, a very inappropriate form of activity. I wish to clear that I do not wish to depend on the goodwill of any lawyer in my defence, if I have to ask for time from that lawyer for my cross-examination. A brief comment on the position of the Prosecution in their motions and submissions regarding the victims and the international community. I know this is on the verge of a procedural issue, but my opinion is that by issuing the indictment this is all part of the legal proceedings which is in the interest of both the victims and the international community, and in that legal proceeding there are two parties, and I wish to say -- state very clearly my Defence supports both the victims and the international community, and that is my position regardless of what is stated in the Statute. I lived with those victims. I was a member of the state government for the last 10 or 15 years in various commissions for the missing persons. I participated in various conferences about these issues, and I know how it functions, or at least I assume I know. There are people sitting here who the moment they received the indictment surrendered, and it never occurred to them to create a story for the media linked to this Tribunal. Unfortunately, that is how to arrest the escaped accused, whereas the quality of the proceedings is being pushed into the background. Also when talking about the international community, we can talk about the apparatus of various international organisations and states, and I consider myself to be a part of that international community with some 3.000 diplomatic contacts covered with reports and notes. So I do have some experience in that area. And I wish to say that the Prosecution does not have a monopoly over the representation of the victims and the international community. An argument is an argument, and it should not be strengthened by reference to victims and the international community. The Trial Chamber consists of professionals, not jurists. Anyway, already -- jurors. I have said that the Prosecution should be given every opportunity to present its case to the end. Judge Trechsel was quite right when he made a distinction last time between the truth and the establishment of guilt. So here we have to establish the truth about the alleged guilt of the six of us. This trial cannot provide the full truth because the method does not allow it. Everything is focused on an individual attracting negative energy while neglecting a series of factors including those who appear as witnesses or authors of documents, which in certain stages could have had far greater significance than those who are here, the accused. Precisely because it is not possible to establish the truth, I am not participating in the trial. For the truth, a multi-disciplinary approach is required, and in such a process I could participate. Of course, even truth commissions cannot establish the truth, even though all the institutions of Bosnia and Herzegovina opted for their formation, but it was upon the intervention of this institution that that process was suspended. So it should be clearly stated regarding the burden of proof. It is not true that the truth is being established in The Hague, which is frequently said in the region. This is not possible, nor is it the task of this Tribunal. I have already said once that regarding the establishment of the truth about guilt, it is very important the way in which the proceedings are conducted. In my opinion, a criterion for the success of the trial is that there is no uncertainty as to what your decision will be, because the trial itself has shown this to everyone following it. Of course I am not in a position to lecture anyone here, nor was I able to follow everything that is happening in connection with this Tribunal. It is my opinion that this proceeding has to be stable, and that -- in that respect I agree with the Prosecutor. You have already said a number of times that this case would not be tried according to our continental law, and I apologise to the Prosecutor. This is a hybrid system, but it must be a stable one. The whole story started with the intervention by my counsel because of interruptions during the cross-examination. I personally consider your questions useful for channeling the discussion for this type of indictment of which you yourself, Judge Antonetti, said it requires 126.000 decisions. So the immediate cause were the interruptions during the limited time given for the Prosecution. Why -- for the cross-examination. I'm sorry. The indictment everyone realises is a political concept. It is a separate diplomatic story which I thought was over in 2004 when we formed the federation. That concept has many elements of the charges against individuals in this trial, but obviously apart from some marginal attempts, it is not believed that the victims of that concept should be represented in the same way, nor in the way as the international community is being represented, because we do not have the same interests. I am not talking about quid pro quo but I am talking about different approaches and elaborating on the thesis about interruptions in the cross-examination. Furthermore, there are stereotypes in the indictment without anyone wondering whether that stereotype has any meaning. This relates to people, members of the international community, diplomats, and journalists. We wish this political concept under A and the stereotype under B to balance these two concepts during the cross-examination. Therefore, the cross-examination and continuity is not an attempt to manipulate witnesses but an attempt to move away from the facts, because the witness will not accept them if they know that they might jeopardise the mentioned political concept or, rather, the accepted stereotype contained in most of their statements and in the so-called proofing sessions. Finally, everything that I have said has not been said because I do not have faith in the Trial Chamber trying this case. I do not wish to use those categories at all, that is whether I trust someone or not, nor should you care about that. What I do expect of you is simply a fair trial and sufficient intellectual courage in making your determinations and nothing more than that. Just as the Tribunal will not be remembered when someone is arrested, so this trial will not be remembered because it is the longest in history, but only by the quality of the proceedings and of the decisions made. I thank the Trial Chamber for the time allotted to me, and I am at your disposal for any clarifications of what I have said, if necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President. Just for the record, there have been some -- I'm told that there are some errors. I'll just read them out, page and line and perhaps that could be looked at, at some other point. Page -- page 7, lines 2 to 3; page 8, line 10; page 15, line 18 to 19; page 16, line 8 and also line 24; and page 13, line -- line 3 and 4. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Thank you, Mr. Prlic, as well. The Chamber noted all that you said and listen to you carefully. We could respond right now, but a debate would surely start. So what we will do, we will render a decision since it is your own counsel that requested all these meetings, and therefore we will render a decision pertaining to procedural questions. But through this decision -- and through this decision we will try as much as possible to answer to what you've said, to answer various points that were part on -- of your submission and mainly the adjudicated facts that were very important to you. You will, in fact, obtain an answer. And Mr. Praljak intervened as well regarding his own view of -- on the matter, and we will then render a decision. So at this stage, the Chamber believes that we should not start a debate right now, a debate which would make all the parties participate. Everything that you've said are known to -- these are facts that are known to us, and you've just shed some more light through your own intervention. We have listened to you carefully, and we will try to address all the issues that you've raised in a decision that will be rendered shortly, since we were waiting to hear submissions from parties before we render our own decision. Now, regarding the next witness, as you know, he will have protective measures and, Mr. Scott, could you please confirm this to us? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can confirm that. But before I turn to this witness -- matters, the Prosecution should have a chance to respond. The Chamber has just -- the President has just indicated that they would render a decision soon. I don't think it would be appropriate to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a bit, just a moment, please. Excuse me, one moment, please, Mr. Scott. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, the Chamber just deliberated on whether you should reply to the intervention of Mr. Prlic, and we believe that if your intervention has to do with new points or if you wish to shed some more light on data that are very well-known to all, then you can intervene, but if you are going to just say the same thing, I think that we will waste time. Only you know what you are going to say to us. We trust that you will do whatever is in the best interests of the justice, but please try to it avoid issues and topics that were already mentioned very many times. And as you know, the Appeals Chamber will render its decision, and we are waiting to actually get the decision from the Appeals Chamber. So you may have the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I must say again that I'm -- I'm rather alarmed that the Chamber would consider proceeding without giving both parties an equal opportunity to be heard, and I'm afraid this is one further instance of a double standard in the courtroom. Defence counsel addressed a number of issues and took substantially greater time than the Prosecution took in the hearings that we had some weeks ago, and apparently it appears to be the Chamber's, or at least some part of the Chamber's view, that the Defence gets two bites at the apple. The lawyers get to talk and then the accused get to talk. And unfortunately my representative victims couldn't be here today, so I will have to speak on their behalf, as I've talked about before. So I -- it's completely unfair and completely wrong procedure to suggest that I would not be given the opportunity to respond to these matters. What one of the -- one of the items that was originally tabled was the participation of the accused in the proceedings, and the Chamber may recall, when these matters were discussed some weeks ago, it then expanded into a broader set of agenda items which all counsel then addressed, and the Chamber or some part of the Chamber, again it may have been at the request of Defence counsel, it may have been on the initiation of the Chamber itself, because the Defence -- because the accused couldn't participate, specifically asked to put the agenda item of the participation of the accused in the questioning of witnesses as a separate agenda item and requested the parties, the counsel, not to address that item. I think the transcript will support me on that. So indeed this is the first time that the Prosecution has had a chance to respond to that, at least in any significant way. We may have given a preview, but the Chamber specifically asked counsel not to address these issues on the previous occasion. Your Honour, I must state in the strongest possible way my objection to any system that gives the Defence, if I can use it again, the analogy of two bites at the apple, and that is why in this -- in this institution except in this Chamber one is either represented by counsel or you -- represent themselves, but I am afraid that what the Chamber has done is created a two-headed creature. For the first time in the history of this Tribunal we have clients -- accused, excuse me, who both represent themselves, a la, perhaps, Slobodan Milosevic, and we have the same person represented by competent counsel in the courtroom. And the Prosecution believes that is not the proper way to proceed. We do object to the participation of the accused and the questioning witnesses, except on a truly, truly exceptional basis, and that is what -- we would ask the Chamber to go back to its original ruling, which this Chamber mentioned on a number of occasions, and that is that only on -- at some showing on a truly exceptional basis that one of the accused be allowed to directly participate in the questioning of witnesses, and that we have moved very, very far afield from that original exceptional circumstance standard. Now, on that topic, and that was the only topic that was on the agenda for today, and I don't understand -- and this has nothing to do -- this is not personal to Mr. Prlic, my comments are not directed to him or him personally, but I see no value, with all respect, in a represented party getting up and talking about purely legal issues, adjudicated acts, agreed facts, protective measures, the admission of documentary evidence, the application of Rule 92 bis. These are all purely legal matters that surely Mr. Karnavas and the other Defence counsel are completely able to deal with. So that was not the agenda items that were put on -- not the agenda item that was even raised. I'm not even sure how I'm supposed to further respond to all these matters that Mr. Prlic has raised putting -- attempting to draw into question established Tribunal practice in many instances over the past 12 or 13 years. And I'm not going to attempt to respond to all of them at this juncture. The Chamber knows the Prosecution's view on the question of time, and I submit again that, as I've said in the past and I'll probably say again in the future, if there's any party in this courtroom today standing in this courtroom this afternoon that has been most prejudiced by limitations on time it is the Prosecution and not the Defence, with all respect to the Defence. It is our case has been limited. It is our ability to present our case that has been limited, and so when I hear it -- once again, when I hear the Defence and I hear the accused talk about the prejudice caused to them and their concerns about limitations on time, I state again our position fourfold. We -- on this particular issue, Your Honour, again to come back to what I understood was the only agenda item to be addressed, and that is the participation of the accused themselves in the questioning of witnesses, it's the Prosecution position that the Chamber should return to its original ruling and that is that such participation would only be allowed on an exceptional circumstance basis. And before I finish on that, I will just mention -- and I will mention it again my comments are not personal to Mr. Praljak, but since Mr. Praljak has been the accused which has spoken perhaps the most, let me just point out that on the vast majority of these matters Mr. Praljak is not uniquely situated as to all accused who have appeared before this Tribunal to talk about these matters. Many military officers, many senior military officers from all three warring parties, Croat officers, Muslim officers, Serb officers, senior officers, Krstic in the Krstic case, the head of the Serb -- one of the senior Serb officers around Srebrenica, others have appeared. Now, they could equally have argued that only they could -- were uniquely situated to put military questions to witnesses in the case. Now, it strikes me as odd and not credible that in all the years of this Tribunal that Mr. Praljak is the first one who is uniquely situated and only he can put his questions to the witness when all of the counsel in all of the cases have been able to do that, apparently quite competently. So once again, Your Honour, I will close with remarks that request that the Chamber return to its original view and that is that participation be limited to an exceptional basis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will need five minutes, maybe less. Probably three. I'll be very laconic on this. First and foremost, the Prosecution asked for time to rebut what Mr. Prlic said and then proceeded to talk about an issue that was directed primarily towards General Praljak. That is a separate issue. That's a much more complex issue that should be debated perhaps at some other point in time and not today. Be that as it may, whether other generals have chosen to participate directly or indirectly during the trial proceedings is irrelevant. What's relevant is that Mr. Praljak has human rights, and he's exercising them. He's entitled to assist in his own defence and also to participate. To the extent the Trial Chamber wishes to curtail those rights, I think at this point in time we do have a decision. I agree with the Prosecution. The decision should be abided by. But I think by and large the Trial Chamber is following the decision. And of course the Prosecution is free to object on grounds of relevancy if the Prosecution feels that Mr. Praljak is going into areas that he shouldn't be going into. And I'm not here to defend Mr. Praljak, but I do wish to point out that this is an added issue. Now, with respect to Mr. Prlic and what Mr. Prlic raised, my client, and of course he didn't get pre-clearance from me but if he had asked for pre-clearance, I mean, it's his skin. At the end of the day he's going to go and face the consequences of your -- of your decision. So obviously, even had I wanted to talk him out of going into procedural issues, which I would not have, I think he's entitled to raise those issues, but I think when you get down to it there was one fundamental issue at stake, and that is: He's asking for a fair trial. What I find supremely ironic, what I find really galling at this point in time is Mr. Scott standing up after Mr. Prlic is fighting for him, for the Office of the Prosecution to have sufficient time to put on their case. And what I don't hear from that side is: Let the Defence have enough time to defend themselves. That's what I find shocking. And that's the whole message that Mr. Prlic was saying, let us have sufficient time to try our case, and trying to bring in all these adjudicated facts is not the way. We are trying to have a trial. This is the longest trial, the most complex trial by their calling. Let us have that. That's what he's asking for. We were not able -- I was not able to thoroughly cross-examine the last witness, Ambassador Okun, primarily because I didn't have enough time and chopping it up isn't enough. You can't do one thorough cross-examination, and as Mr. -- I asked Mr. Prlic, I begged him to fight with the other accused to try to get their time so we could use it, and his answer was, "No, they have rights too." So -- and I was upset at him and I yelled at him my own client nor not fighting to argue with the other accused to give up their time for him because we felt we might have been able to do a more comprehensive cross-examination for everyone, but at the end of the day every accused has their angle, has their defence, and has a right, and in hindsight thinking back, Mr. Prlic was correct. How dare I ask him to ask others to give up their right so he can enjoy more rights? And that's what this is all about. And I think that the Prosecution ought to be standing up here and applauding what Mr. Praljak, Mr. Prlic, and others have said, which is give them more time, but at the same time you should be asking the Trial Chamber to allow all of the accused to have all the time necessary for cross-examination, and I think that's the end of the story. I look forward to your decision. Hopefully we can have a much more relaxed atmosphere by relaxing a little bit the rules, allowing us to do more cross-examination when necessary, and feel free to object. Feel free to step in and tell us -- and ask why is a point relevant and if it's not relevant to cut us off and to force us to move on. I think that's the greatest power that you have in controlling the circumstances here. But barring that, let us go on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think we should not prolong this actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have extensively spoken on the issue of to what extent your client ought to be allowed to cross-examine himself. I have that, and I'm sure the Chamber has that in vivid memory. It's not quite true what Mr. Scott said that if Defence counsel did not reply. Maybe the Chamber did not want them to reply, but they did nevertheless in very strong terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with all due respect, I understand what you've just said and I take it as a limitation, but I have to draw attention to something that Mr. Karnavas, I think, mentioned. The Prosecution in this alleged response to the accused Prlic in fact presented new arguments in major part. So with your permission to have an equality for both sides, I have the right to respond to those new arguments and to add something to the arguments that we put forward earlier on, as you mentioned. I am deeply convinced that this is necessary in order to balance out the process, to strike the proper balance in this courtroom. You will of course make your ruling and decision when you have heard all the arguments, but as new arguments have been put forward here, I have the right to respond to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm interested to hear what you think is a new argument. Frankly, I have not heard any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor in another way, in a different way today, on this occasion and with new arguments, he explained and expounded the thesis according to which the accused when they have counsel to represent them in fact do not have the right directly themselves to take part in the proceedings. That is certainly a new argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, he has exposed this in substance quite clearly. I think we could get along much faster if the parties could agree to complain less about lack of time. It seems as if this Chamber were some institution with a thumbscrew screwing the thumbs of both parties and having a good time. We are as much pressed. We are in a difficult situation, too, and I think it would be time that the parties recognise that we're all in one boat and that we do not gain anything by this constant moaning and complaining and repeating endless times. I wonder how much time would be made if one added all the complaints of lack of time. I think several days probably could have been put to use. And I sometimes doubt whether this is not something that -- that comes close to a delaying tactic, frankly, because we have heard this ad nauseam, frankly. Another point I would like to say, we had given in to Mr. Karnavas's exceedingly forcefully put request that we have a hearing where the Defence can complain about issues in the proceedings they feel that they have to complain about. The Chamber has conceded this. We have also agreed that we would listen to what the accused would have to say, and this was a bit in a humanitarian spirit. They are sitting here all the time. We also want to hear what they say. But that is more in a way of -- of sounding their mind, of having them put their state of mind and feelings to the Chamber. It is not really legal submissions they made, and that is the way in which we have listened to those of the accused who have wished in this context to address the Chamber. I think that we have had all the legal arguments in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with all due respect, I simply cannot and won't accept your arguments, the arguments you put forward about taking time and wasting time. As a man of law, I cannot agree with that. You have all the prerogatives as the Trial Chamber to decide in the matter, and you will make the decision as you have been doing thus far. However, when we're talking about this topic, and we are, and I agree there with you that unfortunately all these legal arguments or the humanitarian spirit and aspects that you mentioned remain an abstract context if in the courtroom we do not have the time to present the arguments that we consider to be relevant and to influence a fair trial in these proceedings. And -- so that is something that I have to respond to. We're all conscious that the essence of everything here is time and we're all fully conscious of the fact that we do not have enough time. However, Your Honours, it is not the accused who constructed this megalomaniac indictment and it is not the accused who compiled an indictment which by its very nature demands reasonable time in order to present evidence to bear out the indictment and -- or not, and to go into the question of procedural rights, which, without a doubt in one way or another to a greater or lesser extent, ultimately effect a fair trial. And a fair trial is the key to all these proceedings. That is what is laid down in the Statute. This is the basic principle that we adhere to in every national court of law and international court of law. And you yourselves frequently say that you're taking steps in order to ensure a fair trial. And I am deeply convinced, Your Honour, out of respect for this Trial Chamber that you're -- you're not saying that in your decisions and verbally declaring that only because it sayings so in the Statute. You are saying that because you are educated lawyers and you know that that is the key to all these proceedings. So may I take a few minutes to respond tomorrow what the Prosecutor said. The Prosecutor starts out from the assumption and that's the crux of the matter, the assumption an accused in the courtroom who has legal representation and counsel, professional counsel, that thereby in that same courtroom ipso facto he becomes the object of the proceedings and as we've seen in the many trials that have already been held is a tactics of the Defence, the accused in 90 per cent of the trials held in this International Tribunal the accused sat quite peacefully for two, three, five years during the legal proceedings without the Judges ever hearing a single word uttered from them, unless asked what their health was like perhaps. So this kind of situation the de facto situation that exists in this it Tribunal is not as a result of the Rules of Procedure and proceedings but of the rights used by the Defence, and it is also the right of the Defence to keep silent. Here we have a different situation. We have six accused who to a greater or lesser extent actively participate in the trial. So that is the argument I would like to respond to. An accused is not the object of the trial, the object of the proceedings; he is the subject and the proceedings are being conducted against him and it is his right to participate in those proceedings in different ways. Institutionalised law. The first right is to -- for counsel to help -- or, rather, the accused to help his counsel by briefing him about facts indicating certain events and so on. But in addition to that right he has the right to take part in the debate itself. Once again let me repeat because he is not an object but a subject, and it is his fate and destiny that is at stake, his head that is on the line; so he has the right to defend himself, not only by appointing counsel and instructing counsel but to take part himself. A, to take part in the cross-examination of witnesses by showing documents. B, taking part to a certain extent in procedural matters when in comes to fundamental questions concerning a fair trial. So the accused, without doubt has these rights regardless of whether he has appointed counsel or not. They can say, "Your Honours, I consider that such-and-such is not fair." That is what an accused has the right to do. It's quite another matter how the Trial Chamber is going to weigh this up, whether they're going to accord the accused this right or not. But accused without a doubt does have the right to speak up. Therefore, would any of us here in this courtroom accept the fact that the trial was a fair trial if we curtail the right of an accused to take the floor if they wish to do so. I don't think it would be a fair trial under those conditions. I will stop there. Of course there are other arguments that can be put forward as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, just for two or three minutes. I have accepted what Your Honours have suggested, that is to comment on technical questions, and I think 90 per cent of my interventions were like that. There were a lot of maps, and my questions related only to matters that in my view should be discussed by a military expert, and he should be here permanently, a social psychologist, a sociologist and a military expert. They should be there permanently. The Judges are professional Judges but they're not military experts. And I had expected the Chamber to tell the Prosecutor that certain generals cannot be tried with -- when bringing the maps of Mostar of the size 10 by 10 centimetres. So this is so inappropriate. So, Mr. Scott, as long as the law gives me that right I will defend myself in a dignified and professional way with maps, facts, trigonometry, and all the knowledge that I've acquired in my life which is not so small.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to prolong things. Good afternoon Mr. President and Your Honours. I don't want to prolong things but speaking as one who represents one of the accused who does not have any interest in representing himself, I do have some observations that are new and may be of assistance. Mr. Scott has made the point that there was a previous ruling of the Trial Chamber as to the extent of the accuseds' representation, but, Your Honour, the fact of the matter is that, I think on the second day of this trial, General Praljak made an opening statement on his own behalf that lasted for a number of hours and ever since there has, without apparent objection, played a very active role in the proceedings. And, Your Honour, we're now a year into trial, and for the Prosecution at this point to change what has in effect become the practice in this trial at this late stage would obviously be highly prejudicial and whatever the objective rights and wrongs of the situation, Your Honour, it's my respectful submission that it's now far too late for -- to go back on that. The train has left the station a considerable time ago and it would place the Praljak Defence, no doubt possibly other accused, in an impossible situation if they had to revise their entire trial strategy at this point. Your Honour, it may be in my submission that it may be as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we're right back to where -- this makes my point. We've now had two -- at least two accused and their counsel both participate today, as if they both have the same amount of time. Now, if I had one of my -- one of the victims sitting here and the could -- the victim can give me his time or her time or whatever, it would be the same thing, and that's -- this is the point that's made. If you look at this, and I've asked my case manager to do this, look at the total time that has been spent on these matters since it was first tabled and the total time, and you will find, I'm sure, that the Prosecution has used substantially less time than the various Defence counsel and the various accused combined. Substantially less. I'm talking by -- by orders of magnitude. And then we -- then we do it again. Then we get up again and then we go through it all over again. Now, just to simply address -- all I'm going to do now is simply address Mr. Murphy's point. Your Honour, I'm happy if the Chamber thinks it would be helpful to take the time to go back for the record. Prosecution has repeatedly objected to Mr. Praljak's interventions on a number -- on many number of occasions. And perhaps we should -- perhaps based on Mr. Murphy's comment, we should have objected even more. I think there is the phenomenon when a party objects and objects and objects and continue -- continuously to no effect, one decides that probably it's not worth -- worth the effort. But it has consistently been the Prosecution's position that the Chamber's original ruling should apply and that is -- and that's been our position all along and we have objected any -- on any number of occasions. And in fact I've heard the Judges object on a number of occasions and ask and tell Mr. Praljak, We don't know where you're going. This seems to us to be a waste of time. And so everyone in the courtroom has objected at times, and our position is simply, like all the other trials that have been conducted to date, and this Chamber is not conducting the first trial at the ICTY, other accused have not participated in this way, and we've -- you've created, I'm sorry, but with great respect you've created a two-headed creature, both counsel, both representing themselves and we think there are exceptional circumstances in which that must be justified, but it shouldn't be day-to-day practice. And that's our submission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is 20 to -- 25 to 4.00. We're going to have a 20-minute break and we will resume work with the hearing of the witness after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, let us go into private session. Will you put the blinds down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 17th day of April, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.57 p.m.,
